I realised a while ago that I'm depressed. I have no interest in ever killing myself, and it's nothing debilitating.

I have no friends. I have roughly 800 on Facebook but none I can call up and say "hey, let's go catch a movie". Without identifying myself, I have a couple hobbies that don't really fit my demographic, so it's difficult to meet friends in any groups or clubs.

My days are very unfulfilling and I get bored incredibly easily. All throughout my life people have been saying how impressed they are that I'm seemingly good at everything with a billion different talents but I've never devoted myself to anything and I haven't mastered anything. It's very difficult to progress with the few things I want to master because I have no direction.

I end up staying up until 4am browsing the most pointless websites in hopes of getting a tiny bit of dopamine, as I'm pretty flatlined otherwise. This has created a haze everyday and I can feel my brain running out of oil. It's difficult to recall things and my brain just generally doesn't work as well.

I don't drink and I'm not a fan of bars and clubs. I'm good with people, alcohol just isn't my thing, even if I'm not the one drinking it.

Anyway, that's my story. What do you folks do to help with your depression, or simply days when you're feeling down? I'm not looking for advice per se, but maybe I can implement things you do to help me
How do you, personally, deal with depression?
I picked up the guitar. Forcing myself to learn an instrument took my mind off all the negative stuff and set me on track to achieve a goal. It really saved my life now that I look back on it.

I identify with some of your feelings, I become depressed and isolate myself from people.

I smoke quite a bit of Marijuana, but in a productive medical sense. A lot of my isolation tendencies come from a back injury and chronic pain. So I illegally but medically smoke MJ, small quantities throughput the day. About 1g of good quality bud I pay $1 per gram for. So in that sense I use it to remove the constant pain and help me be more positive and productive in turn making me less depressed.

But when I'm not suicidal, I indulge in my photography. I've also picked up a hobby of creating digital music. At my worst, Mirtazapine helped me start sleeping and eating again. I'd gone about a month barely eating and sleeping, just sitting at home staring at the wall and self medicating with alcohol. Eventually I sought help and went to the doctors, got the medication I needed, Propanolol and Mirtazapine (ended up with some Diazepam after a manic episode too). I'm now past that point and have come off the medication but like everyone suffer down days and moments of soul crushing lowness / emptiness, but I've found that personally a couple of things help me perk up. I say to myself this is just some emotion that will pass, then try to focus my mind on some form of entertainment, learning or other distraction. Sometimes taking a nap helps.

I'll throw myself into something (a project, hobby, whatever). It seems like the last thing I want to do, but at some point I'll forget about life and be completely tuned in. No music, no Facebook, no phone. Just me and my craft. Sometimes the moment lasts ten minutes, sometimes it lasts hours. Every single time it feels like a gift. Like a warm drug given to me to avoid having to think about whatever is on my mind. It's easy to get get addicted to. And after a week or so I'll wake up excited to chip away and progress further into a project. The hardest part, by far, is starting out.

My advice: Go a full week doing something future you would like to be good at. See how you feel at the end of that week.

Weed helps, so long as I'm not smoking it daily. It makes me weird if I smoke it daily. I watch a lot of Netflix, and play a lot of video games and read a lot of news/science articles to keep my mind off of myself. I started learning a second language, too. It keeps my mind occupied. If the depression is bad enough, I try to go to bed early. Oh, I adopted 2 cats that I have the responsibility of feeding every morning. It forces me out of bed every day. I also started swimming for fitness to try to lose weight. I know my weight contributes to my depression.

I tried anti depressants but the side effects were just too much for me (for example, for me personally, the killing of my libido caused me serious emotional distress to the point of depression... while I was on drugs to take that feeling away). I ended up not being able to handle it and stopped taking them after just a few months.

Mostly, I looked at my weaknesses (refusing to go to sleep, never waking up, constantly worrying) and attempted to treat those issues. Forcing myself to go to sleep manifested as me watching TV in bed until I felt tired enough to sleep. Forcing myself to wake up came in the form of responsibility to feed my cats (my male cat overeats, so I have to feed scheduled meals to keep him from being too fat and costing me money if he develops the beetus). I treat the worrying by my constant occupation of my mind. Language learning, smoking the occasional weed, playing games, making a group of online friends to play said games with, and watching constant television shows. I'm always in the middle of something. (Trailer Park Boys, at the moment).

My biggest suggestions to you would be to find a reason to force yourself to sleep between 12 and 1am. Find something to occupy your time to fill your boredom. Don't worry too much about friends. You'll either find some or you wont. But so long as you feel happy and occupied, your mood will definitely improve. And if you join some stupid group like the gym or some local club, you can have the opportunity to make some friends.

I get listless more than depressive, but perhaps how I deal with it may help. First, I took up exercise. For me, I ride a bike to work every day. I even moved closer to work so I'm guaranteed that exercise every day. I knew if I just did the 'gym thing', I would lose motivation, so I had to build it into my life. That alone has given me new energy, a positive outlook and really improved my happiness quite a bit.

Second, I stopped worrying about friends, getting friends or how many friends I had. My Facebook has 85 people on it. Most of that is family. I cut everyone else out. If I don't talk to you then I don't need you in my feed. There's no competition going on. Most people have one, maybe two 'good friends'. The rest are acquaintances at best. Accept that you don't need 800 Facebook friends to be happy and get rid of them.

Third, pick up a hobby - I know this can be difficult. I am remodeling my house, I work on my bike, I play videos games. I enjoy finding rare craft beers to see how people are experimenting with the craft. All of these are pretty solitary hobbies and they make me damn happy. I would say the biggest happiness improvement was picking up bicycling though.

I used to be in the same situation and I can't stress this enough, exercise. It's a great multi-pronged attack on depression. It releases endorphins make your brain more chemically balanced, you can set yourself goals and feel like you're achieving something and your body will look better making you a little happier ever time you see yourself in a mirror. Best of luck.

I remember that this world around us is so vast that all it takes to see something that will inspire or amaze me is to change my point of view - literally and figuratively. I soon realize that for the most part, most of my dissonance with this world doesn't ACTUALLY have anything to do with me, in the truest sense of the idea. Wars, scandal, politics, conspiracy, greed, injustice - sure, I have a civic responsibility to try to improve these things, but I am a cork bobbing in the ocean. I cannot change those things. What I can change is my point of view. I can go for a car ride and see a beautiful sunset, see the trees whooshing by and feel the wind in my face. I can make an intentional effort to see something new, no matter how small. It can be watching a bug crawling upon the ground and it gives me a sense of how alike we truly are. That bug will never see the majority of the world - just like me, but it keeps going. I have the added benefit though of self-realization and being able to stop working and appreciate the world around me.

To OP - stop staying up until 4am. Don't try to make friends, just talk to people and take genuine interest in them. Not with any agenda of becoming friends with them, just find your own amusement in their stories, what they are about. Soon you will find that those people that you have most in common with are likely going to be your friends. Talk to people about things you think are interesting and live fearlessly. Don't be afraid of rejection. Remember the bug - the world is big and you are small - and so are those that would reject you. There's another hill over that hill.

When our dog was killed 10 years ago -- which I blame myself for -- I slid into a walking dead sort of depression; I was functioning, working like a motherfuker in fact, but got exactly zero joy out of life. For some reason that I no longer recall I tried adding more fat to my diet and it was like a light switch had been flipped back on.

This was about 2007 and precedes the current flavor-of-the-month attention that fats and oils are receiving in the popular media, so please don't discount my comment here are just anther yahoo riding the bandwagon.

I have been consuming a generous tablespoon of coconut oil everyday since then. Without it I'm sure I'd be on medication. If I miss a couple days I can feel those old walls closing in again and it's terrifying. During times of extreme stress even the additional oil isn't enough but I ride it through the rough patch and things return to an even keel once again.

I don't ever feel the same boundless optimism that I had when I was younger though and it appears that for whatever reason that door is closed to me now <shrugs> such is life.

Your mileage may vary, of course, but it's a relatively cheap thing to try and the downside is literally zero, so what have you got to lose? And it beats the fuck out of seeing doctors and taking anti-depression meds.

Either way best of luck; here's hoping you get your life back on track soonest. Cheers!
